title: Tokens and Token Accounts
objectives: Why Solana keeps a token's definition and your balance in separate accounts
What the associated token account is and who pays to create it
Why every on-chain amount is a whole number, and what decimals really do

steps.title: How Solana holds a token balance
steps.body:
The way Solana stores a token balance is a little unusual, and once it clicks, a lot of other behaviour makes sense.

There are two kinds of accounts involved, not one.

The <Term id="mint">mint</Term> is the token itself - the definition. It records the total supply, the <Term id="decimals">decimals</Term>, and which address is allowed to mint more. There is exactly one mint per token, ever. USDC has a single mint account, and every USDC in circulation is accounted for inside it.

Your balance isn't in there. It lives in a separate <Term id="token_account">token account</Term> that your wallet owns, one per token. Your wallet's main address holds SOL and nothing else. The first time you receive USDC, your wallet quietly creates a dedicated account to hold it.

Why split it? Because a wallet can hold hundreds of tokens with different supply rules and different authorities. Giving each one its own account keeps them isolated. Simply put: the mint describes *the asset*, and your token account holds *your slice of it*.

When you receive a new token for the first time, someone pays a small deposit in SOL to create that account - usually the sender. Keep the account and the deposit stays parked. Close it and the SOL comes back.

steps.title: Decimals: why the chain only counts integers
steps.body:
Blockchains don't do decimals. Every validator has to agree on the exact same number, and floating-point arithmetic produces tiny disagreements - the 0.1 + 0.2 kind - that would be fatal at scale. So every balance is stored as a whole number, and a fixed <Term id="decimals">decimals</Term> value tells you where the point goes.

- USDC uses 6 decimals. `1.50 USDC` is stored as `1500000`.
- SOL uses 9 decimals. `1 SOL` is stored as `1000000000` lamports.

Decimals are a display layer. The chain only ever saw the integer, and your wallet does the division to show you something human-readable.

This is also where bizarre numbers come from. If a dapp divides by the wrong power of ten, it asks you to approve a 1,000× amount, or a 0.001× one - and the popup shows it faithfully. When a total looks impossible, the decimals are usually why.

steps.title: Where your token account address comes from
steps.body:
How does an app know which account to send your USDC to, when you never told it? It works the address out.

Your token account is an *associated* token account, and its address is computed from three inputs: your wallet address, the token's <Term id="mint">mint</Term>, and the token program that governs it. Run those through a hash and you get one fixed address - the same for everyone, every time. Nothing is random and nothing is secret.

Technically that makes it a program-derived address (PDA): an address with no private key of its own, derived on demand rather than stored. Which is exactly the point. The app doesn't need a lookup table or a round trip to your wallet - it does the math and has your address.

It's also why you can receive a token you've never held before. The sender's wallet derives your associated account from your address alone, and creates it if it doesn't exist yet.

questions.prompt: If a token has 6 decimals, how is an amount of 2.5 tokens stored on-chain?
questions.explainRight: 2,500,000. Multiply by ten to the power of the decimals: 2.5 × 10^6.
questions.explainWrong: 2,500,000. Balances are integers scaled by 10^decimals, so 2.5 × 10^6.

questions.prompt: What is an associated token account on Solana?
options: A separate bank account in Switzerland
An account your wallet controls that holds your balance for one specific token
questions.explainRight: One account per token, controlled by your wallet - the balance lives there, not in your main address.
questions.explainWrong: It is a dedicated on-chain account that holds your balance for one token mint.
